## Module 1 — Systems foundations (L1–L3)

### L1. Course overview and the IR problem
- Course mechanics: syllabus, grading, the two assignments, the bonus track, and the term project.
- The two faces of every IR system: engineering (latency, throughput, cost) and functional (relevance, coverage, freshness).
- The two phases: indexing (crawl → process → index) and querying (parse → retrieve → rank → serve).
- Offline vs. online evaluation and why both are needed; deployment via A/B testing.
- How requirements bend by use-case: web search vs. e-commerce vs. news vs. ads.
- Crawling in brief: focused crawling, freshness / age-of-cache, data volume, duplicates.

*Example:* a single web-scale query touches an index of billions of pages yet must answer in
~200 ms — the whole course lives inside that relevance-under-a-latency-budget tension.
> **Takeaway:** IR is the disciplined management of a relevance-vs-cost trade-off under a
> latency budget — not a single algorithm.

**Readings**

- `IIR` Ch. 1 — Boolean retrieval and the IR problem.
- `SEIRP` Ch. 1 — search engines in practice.
- Additionall readings 
  - Brin & Page, "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine" — a canonical end-to-end system overview.
  - Olston & Najork, "Web Crawling" (survey) — crawling, focused crawling, and coverage.
  - Cho & Garcia-Molina, "Effective Page Refresh Policies for Web Crawlers" — freshness and age-of-cache.

### L2. System design under constraints
- Wide-area systems: replication, partitioning / sharding, and why one box cannot scale.
- CAP: consistency vs. availability under a network partition; the latency corollary (PACELC).
- Anatomy of a request's latency budget: disk seek+read, cross-continent round trips, fan-out/fan-in.
- Little's law (L = λW) and utilization curves; why latency explodes as utilization → 1.
- Tail latency and fan-out amplification: one slow leaf drags the whole response.
- Case studies: local-master (Yahoo) vs. remote-master (Facebook) replication.

*Example:* a service fanning out to 100 shards, each with a 1-in-100 chance of a slow
response, is very likely to have *at least one* slow shard per query — so the aggregate p99 is
far worse than any single leaf, forcing hedged requests or tighter per-leaf budgets.
> **Takeaway:** There is no one-size-fits-all — every design is a chosen point on a
> consistency/availability/latency/cost surface, and you must name the trade-off you took.

**Readings**

- Brewer, "CAP Twelve Years Later: How the Rules Have Changed" — CAP and its nuances.
- `DDIA` Ch. 5–6 — replication and partitioning/sharding.
- Additional readings
  - Abadi, "Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database Design" — the PACELC refinement.
  - Dean & Barroso, "The Tail at Scale" — fan-out amplification and tail-latency mitigation.
  - Dean, "Achieving Rapid Response Times in Large Online Services" (Google talk) — latency in web-scale services.

- Barroso, Hölzle & Ranganathan, *The Datacenter as a Computer* (Ch. 1–2) — warehouse-scale context.

### L3. Storage and indexing hardware
- The storage hierarchy: cache → RAM → SSD → HDD → network, and their latency/cost orders of magnitude.
- Sequential vs. random access; why a ~10 ms HDD seek dwarfs a streaming read.
- B-Trees: in-place updates; strong reads and range scans; random-write cost.
- LSM-Trees: log-structured writes, compaction, write/read amplification, Bloom filters to skip.
- Choosing by workload: read- vs. write-heavy, point lookup vs. range scan.

*Example:* an inverted-index build is append-heavy, so an LSM-style log beats in-place B-Tree
updates; a user-profile store dominated by point lookups may prefer a B-Tree — the *workload*
picks the structure.
> **Takeaway:** Design to the hardware — sequential access beats random, and logs beat
> in-place updates when writes dominate.

**Readings**

- `DDIA` Ch. 3 — storage engines: B-Trees vs. LSM-Trees.
- Additional readings
  - O'Neil et al., "The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree)" — the original LSM design.
  - Chang et al., "Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data" — a production LSM-backed store.
  - Bloom, "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors" — Bloom filters for skip decisions.
  - Athanassoulis et al., "Designing Access Methods: The RUM Conjecture" — read/update/memory trade-offs.
  - Dong et al., "Optimizing Space Amplification in RocksDB" — LSM compaction and amplification in practice.

## Module 2 — Building a queryable index (L4–L5)

### L4. Text processing, deduplication, and sketching
- Query as a noisy channel: typos, synonymy, and underspecification between intent and tokens.
- Document pre-processing: tokenization, case-folding, stemming/lemmatization, stopwords, phrase/n-gram detection.
- Information extraction: named entities, dates, prices, locations; field weighting (title vs. body).
- Corpus statistics: Zipf's law (term frequency) and Heaps' law (vocabulary growth) → estimating posting-list sizes and ordering conjunctions cheapest-first.
- Deduplication: shingling → sets, Jaccard similarity, and why all-pairs comparison is O(n²).
- Sketching: MinHash (unbiased Jaccard estimator, choosing signature length), LSH banding, SimHash, Bloom filters.

*Example:* two near-identical syndicated news copies share ~95% of their 5-shingles; a 200-hash
MinHash estimates that overlap to within a few percent at a fraction of the storage, and LSH
banding surfaces the pair without comparing it to every other document.
> **Takeaway:** At scale you approximate at sublinear cost — compact signatures replace
> quadratic pairwise work, at a controllable accuracy price.

**Readings**

- `IIR` Ch. 2 — tokenization, normalization, and the term vocabulary.
- `MMDS` Ch. 3 — finding similar items: shingling, MinHash, and LSH.
- Additional readings
  - Broder, "On the Resemblance and Containment of Documents" — MinHash and Jaccard estimation.
  - Charikar, "Similarity Estimation Techniques from Rounding Algorithms" — SimHash.
  - Manku, Jain & Das Sarma, "Detecting Near-Duplicates for Web Crawling" — SimHash at web scale.
  - Sarawagi, "Information Extraction" (survey) — entity/field extraction foundations.
  - Manning, Surdeanu et al., "The Stanford CoreNLP Natural Language Processing Toolkit" — a practical NLP/IE pipeline.

### L5. Inverted index, compression, and query processing *(merged)*
- Inverted index anatomy: dictionary + postings (docIDs, term frequencies, positions).
- Query operators over postings: AND/OR/NOT via merges; phrase/positional and field queries.
- The I/O-vs-compute gap: reading two 1 MB posting lists (~0.05 s) vs. merging them (~0.001 s).
- Compression: d-gap (delta) encoding, then unary, Elias-γ/δ (bit-aligned) and v-byte (byte-aligned); skip pointers for binary search over compressed gaps.
- Query-processing strategies: term-at-a-time vs. document-at-a-time; top-k thresholding (WAND/τ), early termination, result caching.
- Robustness: misspellings and query expansion (Rocchio / pseudo-relevance feedback).
- Query understanding and suggestion: intent classification, spelling correction at scale, query segmentation, entity linking, and autocomplete/typeahead (trie + ranking, session-aware suggestion).
- Near-real-time / streaming indexing: incremental index updates, Lucene-style NRT search, and change-data-capture freshness pipelines.

*Example:* v-byte can shrink a posting list ~4×, so it reads in a quarter of the time;
decompression costs far less than the I/O saved, so throughput rises — compute traded for
bandwidth, exactly the bottleneck that matters.
> **Takeaway:** Compression exists to trade cheap compute for scarce bandwidth; the right code
> depends on where your bottleneck sits in the memory hierarchy.

**Readings**

- `IIR` Ch. 4–6 — index construction, compression, and scoring.
- `SEIRP` Ch. 5 — ranking and query processing.
- `MMDS` Ch. 2 — MapReduce (for distributed index build).
- Additional readings
  - Broder et al., "Efficient Query Evaluation using a Two-Level Retrieval Process" — the WAND top-k algorithm.
  - Ding & Suel, "Faster Top-k Document Retrieval Using Block-Max Indexes" — Block-Max WAND.
  - Lemire & Boytsov, "Decoding Billions of Integers per Second Through Vectorization" — modern posting-list codecs.
  - Cai & de Rijke, "A Survey of Query Auto Completion in Information Retrieval" — autocomplete/typeahead.
  - `DDIA` Ch. 11 — stream processing and near-real-time updates.
  - Bialecki et al., "Apache Lucene 4" — a production near-real-time inverted index.

## Module 3 — Relevance and ranking (L6–L7)

### L6. Ranking models: from heuristics to learning-to-rank
- Boolean retrieval and its all-or-nothing limitation.
- Vector-space model: tf–idf weighting and cosine similarity.
- Probabilistic ranking principle; BM25 with term-frequency saturation and length normalization.
- Language-model view: query/document likelihood with smoothing (Dirichlet, Jelinek-Mercer).
- Query-independent quality priors: PageRank and HITS.
- The pivot to learning: risk minimization; generalization error (irreducible / estimation / approximation); pointwise, pairwise (RankNet), listwise (LambdaMART) objectives; GBDTs as the workhorse.

*Example:* BM25 alone cannot tell that an authoritative page should outrank a keyword-stuffed
one; a learned ranker that *combines* BM25 + PageRank + click features can — which is precisely
why we move from a fixed formula to learning a combination of signals.
> **Takeaway:** Relevance is a modeling choice; classical scorers are special cases of a learned
> ranker, and learning-to-rank buys the ability to fuse many signals.

**Readings**

- `IIR` Ch. 6, 11, 21 — scoring, probabilistic IR, and link analysis.
- Additional readings
  - Robertson & Zaragoza, "The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond" — BM25 derivation and extensions.
  - Zhai & Lafferty, "A Study of Smoothing Methods for Language Models Applied to Ad Hoc Retrieval" — Dirichlet/JM smoothing.
  - Page et al., "The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web" — query-independent priors.
  - Kleinberg, "Authoritative Sources in a Hyperlinked Environment" — HITS.
  - Liu, "Learning to Rank for Information Retrieval" (survey) — pointwise/pairwise/listwise framing.
  - Burges, "From RankNet to LambdaRank to LambdaMART: An Overview" — the workhorse LTR objectives.
  - Friedman, "Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine" — GBDTs.
  - Qin et al., "Are Neural Rankers Still Outperformed by Gradient-Boosted Decision Trees?" — a modern LTR baseline check.

### L7. Signals that feed ranking
- Feature families: query, document, query–document match, and user/context features.
- Behavioral signals and click models: position bias, cascade and examination hypotheses.
- CTR/CVR prediction: logistic regression → factorization machines → deep models (Wide & Deep, DeepFM).
- Sparse categorical features: embeddings and the hashing trick.
- Calibration: why a predicted 0.1 CTR must mean ~10% clicks for ad pricing/bidding to work.
- Head vs. tail regimes: count/behavioral features for frequent queries, semantic features for the cold tail.

*Example:* an item shown only in position 1 looks "high CTR," but that is position bias, not
quality; a click model corrects the estimate so a genuinely better item stuck at position 5 is
not unfairly penalized when it becomes training data.
> **Takeaway:** A ranker is only as good as its signals — and logged signals are biased by what
> was shown, so calibration and de-biasing are first-class concerns.

**Readings**

- Chapelle & Zhang, "A Dynamic Bayesian Network Click Model for Web Search Ranking" — position bias and the DBN model.
- Craswell et al., "An Experimental Comparison of Click Position-Bias Models" — cascade/examination hypotheses.
- Additional readings
  - Rendle, "Factorization Machines" — modeling sparse feature interactions.
  - Cheng et al., "Wide & Deep Learning for Recommender Systems" — memorization + generalization.
  - Guo et al., "DeepFM: A Factorization-Machine based Neural Network for CTR Prediction."
  - McMahan et al., "Ad Click Prediction: a View from the Trenches" — FTRL and production CTR lessons.
  - Weinberger et al., "Feature Hashing for Large Scale Multitask Learning" — the hashing trick.
  - Guo et al., "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks" — calibration and temperature scaling.

## Module 4 — Semantic retrieval (L8–L9)

### L8. Embeddings and semantic search
- From lexical mismatch to semantic matching: "sofa" vs. "couch," cross-lingual queries.
- Dual-encoder (two-tower) models: encode query and document independently into a shared space.
- Training: contrastive loss, in-batch negatives, hard-negative mining.
- Bi-encoder (fast retrieval) vs. cross-encoder (accurate re-ranking) trade-off.
- Hybrid retrieval: fusing lexical (BM25) and dense scores.
- Learned-sparse and late-interaction retrieval: doc2query/docTTTTTquery expansion, SPLADE learned-sparse, and ColBERT/PLAID late interaction — bridging lexical and dense.
- Multimodal / cross-modal retrieval: CLIP-style joint embeddings and visual search (Google Lens, Pinterest Lens).

*Example:* the query "noise-cancelling earbuds for flights" should retrieve a product titled
"wireless ANC in-ear headphones" — zero token overlap, but neighbors in embedding space; a
two-tower retriever finds it where BM25 cannot.
> **Takeaway:** Embeddings turn retrieval into geometry — cold-tail recall comes from matching
> meaning, not tokens, at the cost of a training pipeline and a vector index.

**Readings**

- Karpukhin et al., "Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering" — the two-tower DPR.
- Huang et al., "Embedding-based Retrieval in Facebook Search" — dense retrieval in production.
- Reimers & Gurevych, "Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks."
- Additional readings
  - Xiong et al., "Approximate Nearest Neighbor Negative Contrastive Learning (ANCE)" — hard-negative mining.
  - Izacard et al., "Unsupervised Dense Information Retrieval with Contrastive Learning (Contriever)."
  - Nogueira & Lin, "From doc2query to docTTTTTquery" — document expansion.
  - Formal et al., "SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for First Stage Ranking."
  - Khattab & Zaharia, "ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction" (+ "ColBERTv2" and "PLAID").
  - Gao & Callan, "Condenser / coCondenser" — retrieval-oriented pretraining.
  - Radford et al., "Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP)" — cross-modal embeddings.

### L9. Approximate nearest neighbors at scale
- Why exact NN and kd-trees collapse in high dimensions (curse of dimensionality).
- IVF (coarse quantization) to prune the search space.
- Product quantization (PQ) to compress vectors and approximate distances in memory.
- HNSW graphs: navigable small-world graphs for near-logarithmic search.
- The recall–latency–memory frontier and how each knob (nlist/nprobe, M/efSearch) moves it.
- Vector databases as systems: filtered ANN (ANN + metadata predicates), index freshness/updates, and quantization at the DB layer (Milvus, pgvector, Weaviate).

*Example:* on a billion vectors, exact search is infeasible; IVF-PQ + HNSW returns ~95%
recall@10 in a few milliseconds using a fraction of the raw vectors' memory — trading a few
percent recall for orders of magnitude in speed and RAM.
> **Takeaway:** Recall, latency, and memory form one frontier — ANN is the knob that trades a
> little accuracy for orders-of-magnitude speed and footprint.

**Readings**

- Malkov & Yashunin, "Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using HNSW Graphs."
- Johnson, Douze & Jégou, "Billion-scale Similarity Search with GPUs (FAISS)."
- Jégou, Douze & Schmid, "Product Quantization for Nearest Neighbor Search."
- Additional readings
  - Indyk & Motwani, "Approximate Nearest Neighbors: Towards Removing the Curse of Dimensionality" — LSH foundations.
  - Guo et al., "Accelerating Large-Scale Inference with Anisotropic Vector Quantization (ScaNN)."
  - Wang et al., "Milvus: A Purpose-Built Vector Data Management System" (SIGMOD 2021).
  - Aumüller, Bernhardsson & Faithfull, "ANN-Benchmarks: A Benchmarking Tool for ANN Algorithms."

## Module 5 — Evaluation, practice, and serving (L10–L12)

### L10. Evaluation: offline metrics, human judgments, and LLM-as-judge
- Set metrics: precision, recall, F1, MAP.
- Ranked metrics: MRR and nDCG (gain × discount), and the assumptions each encodes.
- Building test collections: pooling, graded relevance judgments, inter-annotator agreement (κ).
- The offline/online gap: why an nDCG win need not move online engagement.
- LLM-as-judge: pointwise vs. pairwise prompting; agreement with human labels.
- LLM-judge failure modes and fixes: position bias (randomize order), verbosity bias, self-preference bias, ensembling/calibration.

*Example:* swap the order of two candidate answers and an LLM judge often flips its preference
(position bias); averaging both orderings recovers a stable verdict — a vivid reminder that a
judge, human or model, is a biased instrument to be validated before you trust it.
> **Takeaway:** Every metric encodes an assumption about what users want; judges (human or LLM)
> are themselves biased instruments that must be validated before you trust them.

**Readings**

- `IIR` Ch. 8 — evaluation in information retrieval.
- Additional readings
  - Järvelin & Kekäläinen, "Cumulated Gain-based Evaluation of IR Techniques" — (n)DCG.
  - Voorhees, "The Philosophy of Information Retrieval Evaluation" — TREC and pooling.
  - Sanderson, "Test Collection Based Evaluation of Information Retrieval Systems" (survey).
  - Chapelle et al., "Expected Reciprocal Rank for Graded Relevance" — a cascade-aware metric.
  - Zheng et al., "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena."
  - Thomas et al. (Microsoft), "Large Language Models can Accurately Predict Searcher Preferences."
  - Faggioli et al., "Perspectives on Large Language Models for Relevance Judgment."

### L11. Retrieval lifecycle and online experimentation
- The retrieve → filter → rank → blend pipeline: candidate generation, light then heavy rankers, policy filters.
- Feature stores and event DBs; logging; training-serving skew and the data flywheel.
- A/B testing basics: hypothesis, power, minimum detectable effect (MDE), sample size/duration.
- Variance reduction (CUPED); pitfalls: peeking / sequential testing, multiple comparisons, novelty effects.
- Interference and network effects; switchback and cluster-randomized designs; guardrail metrics.
- Interleaving for ranking evaluation: team-draft / probabilistic interleaving — far more sensitive than A/B for ranking changes and standard in web search.

*Example:* an experiment that looks "significant" after being peeked at daily for two weeks is
mostly false positives; fixing the sample size in advance (or using a proper sequential test)
controls the error — the difference between a real win and noise you talked yourself into.
> **Takeaway:** The pipeline — not any single model — is the product; and only a well-designed
> online experiment can tell you whether a change actually helped.

**Readings**

- Kohavi et al., "Online Controlled Experiments and A/B Testing" (KDD tutorial/survey).
- Additional readings
  - `TOCE` — Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (core text).
  - Deng et al., "Improving the Sensitivity of Online Controlled Experiments by Utilizing Pre-Experiment Data (CUPED)."
  - Johari et al., "Peeking at A/B Tests: Why It Matters, and What to Do About It" — always-valid sequential testing.
  - Chapelle et al., "Large-Scale Validation and Analysis of Interleaved Search Evaluation."
  - Radlinski, Kurup & Joachims, "How Does Clickthrough Data Reflect Retrieval Quality?"
  - Bakshy, Eckles & Bernstein, "Designing and Deploying Online Field Experiments (PlanOut)."
  - Uber Michelangelo / Feast documentation — feature stores and training-serving skew.

**+5%**) offers a single option — the **marketplace-simulation full build**, which rebuilds the
Assignment-1 spine on the simulation harness and additionally solves a problem requiring
counterfactuals only the simulation can reveal. Students may use Claude Code or similar assistants,
but the exams probe whether they understand the code paths and theory behind what they built. Each
submission includes a short (≤4 page) **design note**: *what did you build, which choices did you
make and why, and what did you observe?* Full rationale, evaluation gates, and the
viva/individual-effort protocol for Assignment-1 are in `revisions/assignment-1-revision.md`.

### Assignment-1 — News recommendation on EB-NeRD *and* MIND · two components · 10%
Students build a working, measured, reproducible pipeline on **both** news datasets: rank the
candidate articles in an impression by click likelihood, using the user's click history, session
context, and article content.

- **EB-NeRD** (RecSys 2024 challenge, Ekstra Bladet): ~2.7M users, 600M+ impression logs, 120k+
  articles with title/abstract/body and provided article embeddings; demo/small/large bundles let
  teams dial scale gradually.
- **MIND** (Microsoft News dataset, <https://msnews.github.io/>): ~1M users, 160k+ English news
  articles with title/abstract/body and entity annotations, 15M+ impression logs; MIND-small for
  fast iteration.

Both tasks natively exercise all three modelling axes — **lexical** (titles/bodies), **semantic**
(article/text embeddings), and **behavioural** (click history, recency/decay) — and rapid news
decay makes temporal splitting and freshness handling instructive. **Both leaderboards are up**,
so students can submit and verify their solutions against them; topping a board is not a
necessity — though always appreciated — and grading is **never** on leaderboard rank.

**Two components:**

1. **Component-1 — lexical & semantic retrieval · individual · due 27 Aug (at Quiz-1) · 5%.**
   Retrieval over both datasets using **lexical and semantic features**: the reproducible data
   pipeline with a temporal split, lexical (BM25) and embedding-based candidate generation, and
   the offline evaluation harness. Done **individually**.
2. **Component-2 — learning from click-logs · groups of two · due 10 Sep · 5%.** Building on
   component-1: **behavioural signals from the click-logs** — click-history/session features,
   the re-ranker, baseline reproduced then beaten with an ablation, and the serving/scale
   analysis. Done in **groups of two** (two weeks after component-1).

**The common spine (across the two components):**

1. **Reproducible data pipeline** *(C1)* — download → clean → **temporal train/val/test split**
   (never random for interaction data) → a small feature store; one command rebuilds from raw files.
2. **Two-stage retrieve-then-rank** — candidate generation (lexical and/or ANN) to a few hundred
   candidates *(C1)*, then a **re-ranker** (GBDT or a small neural ranker) over engineered
   behavioural features *(C2)*.
3. **Offline evaluation harness** *(C1, extended in C2)* — the official metrics (AUC, MRR,
   nDCG@{5,10}, plus beyond-accuracy: diversity, novelty, coverage) with at least one slice
   (cold-start vs. warm, head vs. tail) and **bootstrap confidence intervals**.
4. **Baseline reproduced, then beaten** *(C2)* — reproduce the official/starter baseline, then one
   principled improvement with an **ablation**; claimed gains must ship a paired bootstrap 95% CI
   that excludes zero.
5. **Serving & scale analysis** *(C2)* — index memory, p99 retrieval latency, and a back-of-envelope
   cost/QPS at a target SLA (a measured local benchmark plus a scaling argument suffices).
6. **Design note (≤4 pages)** *(both, one per component)* — what you built, choices and
   alternatives, observations, and where it breaks at 10×.

**Anti-gaming:** report metrics **with and without features unavailable at serving time** (an
organizer requirement); enforce the behaviour-window boundary; verify no future-click leakage.

**Rubric (10%):** reproducible pipeline + correct temporal evaluation 30% · two-stage system with
all three axes 25% · baseline reproduced + ablated improvement 20% · serving/scale/cost analysis
15% · design-note clarity 10%. Individual effort is checked via a signed component-ownership
matrix, a short per-member viva (explain-and-modify on the live repo), and per-team exam probes.


### Assignment-2 — Approximate nearest neighbors from scratch · pairs · released 15 Aug · due 14 Sep · 10%
Where Assignment-1 wires existing systems, Assignment-2 has student pairs **implement one core
method themselves** to internalize its mechanics: an ANN method (e.g., HNSW *or* IVF + product
quantization) for a given large vector dataset. Benchmark recall@k vs. latency vs. memory against
a brute-force baseline and a reference library (FAISS), and map how the frontier moves as index
parameters vary. Deliverable includes the code, the benchmark, and the design note. 

### Optional for bonus · up to +10% · individually

The bonus track has offers two options: pick a topic and do a _research suvery_ 
and the _marketplace-simulation full build_ (to be released before midsem) worth up to +10% done solo. 
The programming assignment follows the same standards as the assignments (reproducible repo + short design note), is due **20 Nov**, 
and may not double-count project work. Optionally, one can take up writing research survey on any topic chosen with instructor.

**Part 1 — rebuild Assignment-1 on the simulation harness.** Teams must explicitly rebuild
everything in the Assignment-1 spine, but on the marketplace simulation instead of the EB-NeRD
logs: the reproducible data pipeline, a two-stage retrieve-then-rank over
lexical/semantic/behavioural signals (event-store + lexical backend, query corpus + qrels, funnel
metrics), the offline evaluation harness with bootstrap CIs, a semantic/hybrid backend swap with a
seeded bootstrap A/B, and a defended operating point on the recall–latency–memory–cost frontier
under a serving SLA.

**Part 2 — solve a problem that needs counterfactuals.** In addition, teams pick and solve one
problem that requires observing **counterfactuals** — outcomes under actions the logging policy
never took — which the simulation makes directly observable but Assignment-1's fixed logs never
can. Example ideas:

- **Off-policy estimators vs. ground truth** — deploy a target ranking policy in the simulator to
  observe its *true* reward, then measure how far IPS, self-normalized IPS, and doubly-robust
  estimates computed from logs alone deviate from it, as a function of log size and how much the
  target policy diverges from the logging policy. *(L20.)*
- **Position bias & click-model validation** — serve the *same* result list under swapped or
  randomized positions to measure the true position effect, then test whether click models
  (PBM, cascade) recover it correctly from logs alone. *(L7, L10.)*
- **Feedback loops & popularity bias** — retrain the ranker on its own logged clicks over many
  rounds, and compare against the counterfactual world where an exploration policy generated the
  data; quantify popularity amplification and lost catalog coverage. *(L21.)*
- **The true cost of exploration** — replay *identical* user streams under ε-greedy vs.
  Thompson-sampling exploration to measure realized regret and long-run catalog coverage — the
  same users under two policies, observable only in simulation. *(L20.)*
- **Paired A/B on identical sessions** — run control and treatment on the *same* simulated
  users and sessions to observe per-session treatment effects directly, and quantify how much
  variance (and sample size) a standard between-user A/B or interleaving design wastes relative
  to this paired ground truth. *(L10–L11.)*

## Term project

Teams of **up to 3** (groups declared by **30 Aug**) pursue a problem with reasonable _engineering or science complexity_ (possibly a research question) 
in retrieval or recommendation. The project does not have to be an end-to-end system, nor serve a concrete use-case — 
what matters is a sharp, defensible question and a rigorous investigation of it. 

Teams may **extend the marketplace simulation harness** (e.g., the multi-turn dialog or cross-platform-competition scenarios the
harness scaffolds), bring their own dataset and application (product search, news/feed recsys,

- **Problem finalization (by 30 Sep):** a **deeper literature survey**; the problem statement

  working pipeline or experimental setup where feasible.
- **Final (due 20 Nov):** the completed investigation — implementations of the competing
  solutions, ablations, an offline or simulated A/B evaluation where applicable, and a discussion
  of scaling, cost, and failure modes; report + demo + presentation (presentations in the
  preceding weeks).

The project need not span every course thread. Instead, it must take on one hard, possibly
open-ended question — which may sit entirely within a single thread (systems, ML, or
evaluation) — and explore and evaluate several competing solutions to it in depth. The bar is the
difficulty of the question and the rigor of the study, not breadth of coverage. 
It can either be engineering or science focused.

### Project ideas

Scoped prototypes; evaluation plan agreed with the instructor first:

- **Conversational search** — multi-turn retrieval with query rewriting, clarifying questions, and
  session state; evaluate on a conversational IR benchmark (e.g., TREC CAsT/iKAT). 
- **Agentic memory** — a long-term memory layer for a search/recommendation agent (episodic store,
  retrieval, consolidation); measure the personalization lift over a memoryless agent. 
- **Scouting agents** — standing-query web monitors in the style of Yutori
  (<https://yutori.com/>): persistent user intents, change detection over recrawls, and ranked
  notifications; evaluate alert precision and timeliness. 
- **Generative retrieval (DSI-lite)** — train a small model mapping queries to docIDs on a modest
  corpus; compare against BM25/dense and study behaviour under index updates. 
- **RAG evaluation harness** — chunking + hybrid retrieval + rerank + generate, with RAGAS-style
  grounding and answer-quality evaluation.

"""Load and validate pipeline configuration from a YAML file.

Every module in this project reads its settings from a config file instead of
hardcoded paths, so the same code can run against a different dataset (MIND
vs. EB-NeRD) or a different machine just by pointing at a different YAML file.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import dataclasses
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

# Keys every config file must define. Listed explicitly (rather than inferred
# from the dataclass) so a missing key produces one clear error message here,
# instead of a confusing AttributeError deep inside some later module.
REQUIRED_KEYS = ("dataset_name", "raw_dir", "interim_dir", "processed_dir", "random_seed")


@dataclasses.dataclass
class PipelineConfig:
    """Typed view of a dataset's pipeline configuration.

    Path fields are absolute: load_config() resolves them relative to the
    project root, not the caller's current working directory, so a script
    behaves the same whether it's run from the repo root or from scripts/.
    """

    dataset_name: str
    raw_dir: Path
    interim_dir: Path
    processed_dir: Path
    random_seed: int


def load_config(config_path: str | Path) -> PipelineConfig:
    """Read a YAML config file and return a validated PipelineConfig.

    Args:
        config_path: Path to a YAML file, e.g. "configs/mind_small.yaml".

    Returns:
        A PipelineConfig with all paths resolved to absolute paths.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: if config_path does not exist.
        ValueError: if a required key is missing from the file.
    """
    config_path = Path(config_path).resolve()
    if not config_path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config file not found: {config_path}")

    with open(config_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        raw = yaml.safe_load(f)

    missing_keys = [key for key in REQUIRED_KEYS if key not in raw]
    if missing_keys:
        raise ValueError(f"Config file {config_path} is missing required keys: {missing_keys}")

    # A config file lives at <project_root>/configs/<name>.yaml, so the
    # project root is two levels up. Anchoring relative paths here (rather
    # than at the caller's cwd) is what makes the pipeline reproducible
    # regardless of which directory a script is invoked from.
    project_root = config_path.parent.parent

    return PipelineConfig(
        dataset_name=raw["dataset_name"],
        raw_dir=(project_root / raw["raw_dir"]).resolve(),
        interim_dir=(project_root / raw["interim_dir"]).resolve(),
        processed_dir=(project_root / raw["processed_dir"]).resolve(),
        random_seed=int(raw["random_seed"]),
    )

from pathlib import Path

import pytest

from news_reco.utils.config import load_config

PROJECT_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
MIND_CONFIG = PROJECT_ROOT / "configs" / "mind_small.yaml"


def test_load_config_reads_all_fields():
    config = load_config(MIND_CONFIG)
    assert config.dataset_name == "mind_small"
    assert config.random_seed == 42


def test_load_config_resolves_paths_to_absolute():
    config = load_config(MIND_CONFIG)
    assert config.raw_dir.is_absolute()
    assert config.raw_dir == PROJECT_ROOT / "data" / "raw" / "mind_small"


def test_load_config_missing_file_raises():
    with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
        load_config(PROJECT_ROOT / "configs" / "does_not_exist.yaml")


def test_load_config_missing_key_raises(tmp_path):
    # Write a broken config under a fake "configs/" folder so load_config's
    # project-root resolution (config_path.parent.parent) still has a real
    # Path to compute against, even though nothing else in tmp_path exists.
    fake_configs_dir = tmp_path / "configs"
    fake_configs_dir.mkdir()
    broken_config = fake_configs_dir / "broken.yaml"
    broken_config.write_text("dataset_name: broken\n", encoding="utf-8")

    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="missing required keys"):
        load_config(broken_config)

# Engineering log — Assignment 1, Component 1

Running notes kept per milestone: design decisions, observations, limitations,
and future improvements. This feeds the final ≤4-page design note; it is not
the design note itself.

---

## Milestone 0 — Environment & project scaffolding (2026-08-02)

**What was built**
- Installed Python 3.12.10 via winget (machine had no Python previously).
- Repo skeleton: `configs/`, `data/{raw,interim,processed}/`,
  `src/news_reco/{data,splitting,features,retrieval/{lexical,semantic},evaluation,reranking,utils}/`,
  `scripts/`, `tests/`, `notebooks/`, `reports/`.
- `pyproject.toml` (setuptools, src-layout) + `.venv` + `requirements.txt`
  (pandas, pyarrow, numpy, PyYAML, pytest) + editable install (`pip install -e .`).
- `src/news_reco/utils/config.py`: `load_config()` reads a YAML file, validates
  required keys, and resolves relative paths to absolute paths anchored at the
  project root (not the caller's cwd).
- `configs/mind_small.yaml`: first dataset config (paths + random_seed).
- `tests/test_config.py`: 4 tests, all passing.
- `git init` + `.gitignore` (excludes `data/{raw,interim,processed}/`, `.venv/`
  — nothing committed yet, no commit requested).

**Design decisions**
- **venv + pip over conda/Poetry** — least ceremony, matches the assignment's
  "avoid unnecessary abstractions" instruction; pinned `requirements.txt` is
  enough reproducibility at this project's scale. (Student's explicit choice.)
- **Dict-free config object**: `load_config()` returns a typed `PipelineConfig`
  dataclass rather than a raw dict, so a typo'd field name fails at load time
  with a clear message instead of a `KeyError` deep inside some later module.
- **Paths resolved relative to project root, not cwd**: a config file at
  `configs/<name>.yaml` treats its own grandparent directory as the project
  root. This is what makes `python scripts/whatever.py` behave identically
  whether launched from the repo root or from inside `scripts/`.

**Observations**
- The tool environment used to set this up only reports an integrated Intel
  UHD 770 GPU (`Win32_VideoController` / no `nvidia-smi`) — this doesn't match
  the student's stated 8GB-VRAM desktop, so GPU availability must be
  re-verified directly at Milestone 7 (semantic retrieval), not assumed now.
- `winget`-installed Python does not appear on `PATH` within an already-open
  shell session; each new shell invocation needs `$env:Path` refreshed from
  the Machine/User environment, or must call `.venv\Scripts\python.exe`
  directly by path.

**Limitations**
- `revisions/assignment-1-revision.md` (referenced by the course README for
  full evaluation gates and the viva/individual-effort protocol) is not

## Milestone 0 complete — Environment & project scaffolding

**What was implemented**
- Python 3.12.10 (was missing entirely — installed via winget) and verified.
- Project skeleton: `configs/`, `data/{raw,interim,processed}`, a `src/news_reco/` package with subpackages for `data`, `splitting`, `features`, `retrieval/{lexical,semantic}`, `evaluation`, `reranking` (empty, reserved for Component 2), and `utils`; plus `scripts/`, `tests/`, `notebooks/`, `reports/`.
- `.venv` + `requirements.txt` (pandas, pyarrow, numpy, PyYAML, pytest) + editable install of the package itself (`pip install -e .`), so `import news_reco...` works from any script or test regardless of working directory.
- [config.py](src/news_reco/utils/config.py): reads a YAML file, validates required keys, and resolves relative paths to absolute ones anchored at the project root.
- [mind_small.yaml](configs/mind_small.yaml): first dataset config.
- [test_config.py](tests/test_config.py): 4 tests — all passing.
- `git init` + `.gitignore` (excludes `data/{raw,interim,processed}`, `.venv`) — nothing committed, since you haven't asked for a commit yet.
- [engineering_log.md](reports/engineering_log.md) — started now, one entry per milestone from here on.

**Why this design**
A config-driven, dataset-agnostic package skeleton is the direct enabler of the MIND-first/EB-NeRD-second plan you approved: nothing under `src/news_reco/` will ever hardcode "MIND" — only the config file and a later dataset adapter will differ. The config loader validates eagerly (at load time) rather than letting bad config surface as a confusing error three modules later — cheap now, saves debugging time all project long.

**Alternative considered**
A flat script with argparse flags instead of YAML configs + a loader module. It would work for one dataset, but every new setting (split dates, retrieval params) becomes another CLI flag threaded through every script, and there's nowhere to keep the two datasets' settings side-by-side for comparison — exactly the "small feature store... one command rebuilds" and "modular enough for Component 2" requirements push against that.

**Trade-off accepted**
The src-layout + `pyproject.toml` + editable install is one extra piece of ceremony versus just running scripts from the repo root with `sys.path` hacks. I judged it worth it here because it's a one-time cost that pays off every time we add a new module (no import-path debugging later), and it's what "organized like an open-source project" concretely means.

**What this module does, in short:** turns a YAML file into a validated, typed object with absolute paths, so every later script gets `raw_dir`/`interim_dir`/`processed_dir` without hardcoding or caring where it was launched from.
**Data flow:** `configs/mind_small.yaml` → `load_config()` → `PipelineConfig` object → consumed by every future module (data ingestion, splitting, feature store, retrieval) instead of literal path strings.

**How to verify it yourself**
```bash
cd "C:\shambo.roy@iiit.ac.in\Assignment 1"
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest tests\test_config.py -v
```
You should see 4 passed.

---

Waiting for your approval before starting **Milestone 1** (MIND-small acquisition — you'll need to download it manually and accept Microsoft's research license; I'll give exact steps once you confirm).

input.content:
"""Download and extract the MIND-small dataset from its Hugging Face mirror.

MIND-small is hosted on a gated Hugging Face dataset repo (yjw1029/MIND), so
downloading requires an authenticated Hugging Face account that has been
granted access. Run `huggingface-cli login` yourself first, interactively, in
your own terminal -- this script never asks for or handles your token; it
relies on huggingface_hub picking up the credential huggingface-cli cached
locally on your machine.

Usage:
    python scripts/download_mind_small.py --config configs/mind_small.yaml
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

from news_reco.utils.config import load_config

# The official MIND page (msnews.github.io) points both its "Training Set"
# and "Validation Set" buttons, under the MIND-small section, at this repo.
HF_REPO_ID = "yjw1029/MIND"
HF_FILENAMES = {
    "train": "MINDsmall_train.zip",
    "dev": "MINDsmall_dev.zip",
}


def download_and_extract_split(split_name: str, filename: str, raw_dir: Path) -> None:
    """Download one MIND-small split (train or dev) and unzip it in place.

    Args:
        split_name: "train" or "dev" -- used only to name the output folder.
        filename: The zip filename on the Hugging Face repo.
        raw_dir: Directory under which raw_dir/<split_name>/ is created.
    """
    print(f"Downloading {filename} ...")
    # hf_hub_download caches the file under the user's local HF cache and
    # returns the path to it. It reuses huggingface-cli's cached login token
    # automatically -- no credential is passed or read by this script.

"""Load raw MIND TSV files into pandas DataFrames.

MIND ships two flat files per split (train/dev): news.tsv (article
metadata) and behaviors.tsv (impression logs). Both are tab-separated with
no header row, so column names are supplied here based on the official
MIND data format -- verified directly against the downloaded files, not
assumed from documentation.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

NEWS_COLUMNS = [
    "news_id",
    "category",
    "subcategory",
    "title",
    "abstract",
    "url",
    "title_entities",
    "abstract_entities",
]

BEHAVIORS_COLUMNS = [
    "impression_id",
    "user_id",
    "time",
    "history",
    "impressions",
]


def load_news(news_path: str | Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load news.tsv into a DataFrame with one row per article.

    `title_entities` and `abstract_entities` are left as raw JSON strings --
    parsing them is deferred to whichever later module actually needs entity
    information, so this loader stays a thin, fast I/O layer.
    """
    return pd.read_csv(
        news_path,
        sep="\t",
        header=None,
        names=NEWS_COLUMNS,
        dtype={"news_id": str, "category": str, "subcategory": str},
    )


def load_behaviors(behaviors_path: str | Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load behaviors.tsv into a DataFrame with one row per impression.

    `history` and `impressions` are left as raw space-separated strings --
    exploding `impressions` into one row per (article, clicked) pair happens
    during cleaning (Milestone 2), not here, since that's a bigger decision
    about the impression-candidate table's shape.
    """
    df = pd.read_csv(
        behaviors_path,
        sep="\t",
        header=None,
        names=BEHAVIORS_COLUMNS,
        dtype={"impression_id": int, "user_id": str},
    )
    # MIND timestamps look like "11/11/2019 9:05:58 AM". Parsing here (rather
    # than leaving it a string) is what lets Milestone 3's temporal split
    # compare impressions by actual time, not lexicographic string order.
    df["time"] = pd.to_datetime(df["time"], format="%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p")
    return df

"""Audit the raw MIND-small files: shapes, date ranges, and basic sanity checks.

This is Milestone 1's verification step -- it doesn't clean or transform
anything, it just reports what's actually in the raw files so later
milestones (cleaning, temporal splitting) are built against facts, not
assumptions about the dataset.

Usage:
    python scripts/audit_mind_raw.py --config configs/mind_small.yaml
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
from pathlib import Path

from news_reco.data.mind_loader import load_behaviors, load_news
from news_reco.utils.config import PipelineConfig, load_config


def audit_split(split_name: str, news_path: Path, behaviors_path: Path) -> None:
    """Print shape, date-range, and label-sanity facts for one split."""
    news = load_news(news_path)
    behaviors = load_behaviors(behaviors_path)

    print(f"\n=== {split_name} ===")
    print(f"news.tsv:      {len(news):,} articles, {news['category'].nunique()} categories")
    print(f"  missing abstract: {news['abstract'].isna().sum():,} / {len(news):,}")
    print(f"behaviors.tsv: {len(behaviors):,} impressions, {behaviors['user_id'].nunique():,} unique users")
    print(f"  time range: {behaviors['time'].min()}  to  {behaviors['time'].max()}")

    # Sanity-check the "NewsID-label" format in a sample before any later
    # module relies on it: every label must be exactly "0" or "1".
    sample_impressions = behaviors["impressions"].head(1000).str.split()
    all_labels = {pair.rsplit("-", 1)[1] for row in sample_impressions for pair in row}
    print(f"  impression labels seen in first 1,000 rows: {sorted(all_labels)}")

    empty_history = behaviors["history"].isna().sum()
    print(f"  impressions with empty click history (cold-start candidates): {empty_history:,} / {len(behaviors):,}")


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--config", required=True, help="Path to a dataset YAML config.")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    config: PipelineConfig = load_config(args.config)

    audit_split(
        "train",
        config.raw_dir / "train" / "MINDsmall_train" / "news.tsv",
        config.raw_dir / "train" / "MINDsmall_train" / "behaviors.tsv",
    )
    audit_split(
        "dev",
        config.raw_dir / "dev" / "MINDsmall_dev" / "news.tsv",
        config.raw_dir / "dev" / "MINDsmall_dev" / "behaviors.tsv",
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Audit the raw MIND-small files: shapes, date ranges, and basic sanity checks.

This is Milestone 1's verification step -- it doesn't clean or transform
anything, it just reports what's actually in the raw files so later
milestones (cleaning, temporal splitting) are built against facts, not
assumptions about the dataset.

Usage:
    python scripts/audit_mind_raw.py --config configs/mind_small.yaml
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
from pathlib import Path

from news_reco.data.mind_loader import load_behaviors, load_news
from news_reco.utils.config import PipelineConfig, load_config


def audit_split(split_name: str, news_path: Path, behaviors_path: Path) -> None:
    """Print shape, date-range, and label-sanity facts for one split."""
    news = load_news(news_path)
    behaviors = load_behaviors(behaviors_path)

    print(f"\n=== {split_name} ===")
    print(f"news.tsv:      {len(news):,} articles, {news['category'].nunique()} categories")
    print(f"  missing abstract: {news['abstract'].isna().sum():,} / {len(news):,}")
    print(f"behaviors.tsv: {len(behaviors):,} impressions, {behaviors['user_id'].nunique():,} unique users")
    print(f"  time range: {behaviors['time'].min()}  to  {behaviors['time'].max()}")

    # Sanity-check the "NewsID-label" format in a sample before any later
    # module relies on it: every label must be exactly "0" or "1".
    sample_impressions = behaviors["impressions"].head(1000).str.split()
    all_labels = {pair.rsplit("-", 1)[1] for row in sample_impressions for pair in row}
    print(f"  impression labels seen in first 1,000 rows: {sorted(all_labels)}")

    empty_history = behaviors["history"].isna().sum()
    print(f"  impressions with empty click history (cold-start candidates): {empty_history:,} / {len(behaviors):,}")


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--config", required=True, help="Path to a dataset YAML config.")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    config: PipelineConfig = load_config(args.config)

    audit_split(
        "train",
        config.raw_dir / "train" / "MINDsmall_train" / "news.tsv",
        config.raw_dir / "train" / "MINDsmall_train" / "behaviors.tsv",
    )
    audit_split(
        "dev",
        config.raw_dir / "dev" / "MINDsmall_dev" / "news.tsv",
        config.raw_dir / "dev" / "MINDsmall_dev" / "behaviors.tsv",
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from news_reco.utils.config import load_config

## Milestone 1 — MIND-small acquisition & raw schema audit (2026-08-02)

**What was built**
- Verified the real MIND-small download path by inspecting msnews.github.io's
  DOM directly: both buttons now point to a **gated Hugging Face repo**
  (`yjw1029/MIND`), not the Azure blob storage URLs from older tutorials —
  the Azure Open Datasets catalog entry for MIND has been retired (redirects
  to a generic docs page). Student created an HF account, requested access,
  and ran `huggingface-cli login` in their own terminal — token never seen
  or handled in this session.
- `scripts/download_mind_small.py`: downloads `MINDsmall_train.zip` /
  `MINDsmall_dev.zip` via `huggingface_hub.hf_hub_download` (reuses the
  cached CLI login, no explicit token handling in code) and extracts them.
- `src/news_reco/data/mind_loader.py`: `load_news()` / `load_behaviors()` —
  thin pandas readers with column names and dtypes confirmed by reading the
  raw files directly (not from memory of MIND's docs).
- `tests/test_mind_loader.py`: schema tests, skipped (not failed) if the
  raw data isn't present, so the test suite still runs green for anyone
  without the dataset downloaded.
- `scripts/audit_mind_raw.py`: prints shape, date range, and label-sanity
  checks per split.

**Design decisions**
- **Loaders leave `history`/`impressions`/entity-JSON as raw strings** rather
  than parsing them into structured columns at load time. Reason: exploding
  `impressions` into one row per (article, clicked) pair is a real modeling
  decision (Milestone 2's job — it defines the shape of the interaction
  table everything downstream depends on), not something to bury inside a
  generic "loader."
- **Tests skip rather than fail when data is absent**, so `pytest` stays a
  valid whole-repo verification command regardless of whether the (large,
  license-gated) dataset happens to be present on a given machine.

**Observations (facts, not assumptions — will drive Milestone 3)**
- MIND-small train: 156,965 impressions, 50,000 users, 51,282 articles, 17
  categories. Time range **2019-11-09 → 2019-11-14** (6 days).
- MIND-small dev: 73,152 impressions, same 50,000 users, 42,416 articles.
  Time range **2019-11-15 → 2019-11-15** (exactly 1 day) — dev is literally
  the calendar day immediately after train ends. This confirms train/dev are
  already temporally disjoint by construction; Milestone 3 will treat
  official `dev` as our held-out **test** set and carve **validation** from
  the tail of official `train`, rather than reshuffling the two pools.
- `abstract` is missing for ~5% of articles in both splits (2,666/51,282
  train, 2,021/42,416 dev) — cleaning (Milestone 2) needs an explicit
  decision on how BM25/embeddings handle a missing abstract, not a silent
  NaN-concatenation.
- ~2–3% of impressions have empty click history (`history` is NaN) — these
  are the cold-start cases the rubric's required slice (cold-start vs. warm)
  will use.
- Every sampled impression label is exactly "0" or "1" — no malformed rows
  found in the first 1,000 checked per split.

**Limitations**
- Label sanity check only samples the first 1,000 rows per split, not the
  full file (156,965 / 73,152 rows) — cheap now, full-file validation should
  happen once in Milestone 2's cleaning step, not repeated on every audit run.
- Entity embeddings (`entity_embedding.vec`) cover named entities only, not
  whole-article content — confirmed by inspection. MIND does not ship
  article-level embeddings the way EB-NeRD does; Milestone 7 (semantic
  retrieval) will need to compute our own sentence embeddings over
  title+abstract text for MIND specifically.

**Next**
- Milestone 2: cleaning & normalization into the common schema (articles
  table, interactions table), including an explicit missing-abstract policy.

# Engineering log — Assignment 1, Component 1

Running notes kept per milestone: design decisions, observations, limitations,
and future improvements. This feeds the final ≤4-page design note; it is not
the design note itself.

---

## Milestone 0 — Environment & project scaffolding (2026-08-02)

**What was built**
- Installed Python 3.12.10 via winget (machine had no Python previously).
- Repo skeleton: `configs/`, `data/{raw,interim,processed}/`,
  `src/news_reco/{data,splitting,features,retrieval/{lexical,semantic},evaluation,reranking,utils}/`,
  `scripts/`, `tests/`, `notebooks/`, `reports/`.
- `pyproject.toml` (setuptools, src-layout) + `.venv` + `requirements.txt`
  (pandas, pyarrow, numpy, PyYAML, pytest) + editable install (`pip install -e .`).
- `src/news_reco/utils/config.py`: `load_config()` reads a YAML file, validates
  required keys, and resolves relative paths to absolute paths anchored at the
  project root (not the caller's cwd).
- `configs/mind_small.yaml`: first dataset config (paths + random_seed).
- `tests/test_config.py`: 4 tests, all passing.
- `git init` + `.gitignore` (excludes `data/{raw,interim,processed}/`, `.venv/`
  — nothing committed yet, no commit requested).

**Design decisions**
- **venv + pip over conda/Poetry** — least ceremony, matches the assignment's
  "avoid unnecessary abstractions" instruction; pinned `requirements.txt` is
  enough reproducibility at this project's scale. (Student's explicit choice.)
- **Dict-free config object**: `load_config()` returns a typed `PipelineConfig`
  dataclass rather than a raw dict, so a typo'd field name fails at load time
  with a clear message instead of a `KeyError` deep inside some later module.
- **Paths resolved relative to project root, not cwd**: a config file at
  `configs/<name>.yaml` treats its own grandparent directory as the project
  root. This is what makes `python scripts/whatever.py` behave identically
  whether launched from the repo root or from inside `scripts/`.

**Observations**
- The tool environment used to set this up only reports an integrated Intel
  UHD 770 GPU (`Win32_VideoController` / no `nvidia-smi`) — this doesn't match
  the student's stated 8GB-VRAM desktop, so GPU availability must be
  re-verified directly at Milestone 7 (semantic retrieval), not assumed now.
- `winget`-installed Python does not appear on `PATH` within an already-open
  shell session; each new shell invocation needs `$env:Path` refreshed from
  the Machine/User environment, or must call `.venv\Scripts\python.exe`
  directly by path.

**Limitations**
- `revisions/assignment-1-revision.md` (referenced by the course README for
  full evaluation gates and the viva/individual-effort protocol) is not
  available to the student and was not used in planning. If it surfaces later
  and contradicts anything here (e.g. specific leakage-check requirements),
  those decisions may need revisiting.
- No dataset has been downloaded yet; `data/raw/mind_small/` is an empty
  placeholder directory.

**Next**
- Milestone 1: MIND-small acquisition (student downloads manually — license
  acceptance required) + raw schema audit.

## Milestone 1 complete — MIND-small acquisition & raw schema audit

**What was implemented**
- [download_mind_small.py](scripts/download_mind_small.py): fetches MIND-small via the authenticated `huggingface_hub` cache and extracts it — ran successfully, `data/raw/mind_small/{train,dev}/` now has real data.
- [mind_loader.py](src/news_reco/data/mind_loader.py): `load_news()` and `load_behaviors()`, thin pandas readers with columns confirmed by reading the actual raw files, not documentation.
- [audit_mind_raw.py](scripts/audit_mind_raw.py) + [test_mind_loader.py](tests/test_mind_loader.py): verification.

**Audit results** (facts we'll design around, not assumptions):
- Train: 156,965 impressions / 50,000 users / 51,282 articles / 17 categories, **2019-11-09 → 2019-11-14**.
- Dev: 73,152 impressions, same 50,000 users, 42,416 articles, **2019-11-15 only** — one calendar day, immediately after train ends.
- ~5% of articles are missing an abstract in both splits.
- ~2–3% of impressions have empty click history (cold-start).
- Entity embeddings only cover named entities, not whole articles — MIND doesn't ship article-level embeddings the way EB-NeRD does, so Milestone 7 will need to compute our own.

**Why this design**
The dev split being exactly one day after train, with zero overlap, isn't an accident — it's evidence MIND's own organizers already built it as a temporal holdout. That directly resolves how Milestone 3 should work: treat official `dev` as our **test** set, and carve **validation** from the tail of official `train`, rather than pooling everything and re-splitting ourselves. Discovering this now (via the audit) rather than assuming it means M3 is built on a verified fact.

**Alternative considered**
Parse `history`/`impressions` into fully exploded, structured columns right inside the loader (one row per candidate article per impression). Rejected for now: that reshaping is a real modeling decision — it fixes the shape of the interaction table every later module depends on — and belongs in Milestone 2 (cleaning), not buried as a side-effect of "just loading a file."

**Trade-off accepted**
Tests are skipped (not failed) when the raw data isn't present, so `pytest` on a clean checkout without the (large, license-gated) dataset still passes. The cost: a green test suite doesn't by itself prove the loader works — you have to actually run it once against real data, which we did above.

**What this module does, in short:** turns MIND's raw tab-separated files into typed DataFrames and reports their real shape/date-range/label facts, without transforming anything yet.
**Data flow:** `data/raw/mind_small/{train,dev}/.../*.tsv` → `mind_loader.load_news()`/`load_behaviors()` → pandas DataFrames → consumed by `audit_mind_raw.py` now, and by Milestone 2's cleaning step next.

```bash
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest tests\test_mind_loader.py -v
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\audit_mind_raw.py --config configs\mind_small.yaml
```

The core idea is to design a unified articles table and interactions table that standardizes everything, then figure out what needs to happen to make that work.

For the articles table, I need to map dataset-specific IDs to canonical ones and include fields like category, subcategory, title, abstract, and published time — but here's a problem: MIND's news.tsv doesn't actually include article publish timestamps, only entities, title, abstract, and URL. This creates a real issue for my original plan around time-gating candidate pools to prevent leakage. I need to rethink how freshness and leakage prevention work specifically for MIND since we don't have that timestamp signal.

The best proxy available is using the earliest time an article appears in the behavioral logs — either in user history or impression candidate lists — as a "first seen" signal rather than true publish time. This is a meaningful limitation compared to datasets like EB-NeRD that have explicit published and modified timestamps. I could either skip time-gating for MIND entirely and treat the full news corpus as available for any impression, or use this behavioral proxy, but either way it's a design decision worth flagging. Now I'm thinking through the interactions table structure — exploding each impression into individual rows for each candidate shown, with a clicked label. This gives us the right granularity for metrics and evaluation. I'll keep user history separate as a compact structure (either a dedicated table or a list column per impression) so we can identify warm versus cold-start users and have it ready for behavioral features later, and the feature store scaffolding we've already set up will come into play once we hit the temporal split milestone.

The article catalog is actually defined by what appears in each split's impressions rather than being a fixed universal set, so I need to merge the train and dev news files while deduplicating by article ID to get the complete known catalog. Option A (keep everything, concatenate gracefully) is the standard approach in information retrieval and doesn't warrant dropping real catalog items just for a missing optional field — this feels like the clear choice rather than a genuinely competitive design decision.

The real consequential call is around freshness and leakage-gating given the lack of publish timestamps in the data, which deserves full consideration. For the interactions table, I'm thinking through whether to store the user's prior article history as a list per impression row or handle it differently, since that history gets repeated across every candidate article for the same impression.

The better approach is normalizing into separate tables: an `impressions` table at impression granularity with impression_id, user_id, time, and history, plus an `interactions` table at candidate granularity with impression_id, candidate_article_id, and clicked — joinable by impression_id. """Transform raw MIND DataFrames into the project's common schema.

The common schema is dataset-agnostic: three tables (articles, impressions,
interactions) with the same column names regardless of whether the source
was MIND or (later) EB-NeRD. Every module downstream of this one is written
against news_reco.data.schema, not against MIND's raw tsv format.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import pandas as pd

from news_reco.data.schema import ARTICLES_COLUMNS, IMPRESSIONS_COLUMNS, INTERACTIONS_COLUMNS


def build_articles_table(*news_frames: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Union one or more raw MIND news.tsv frames into one article catalog.

    MIND's news.tsv is scoped per split -- train/dev each list only the
    articles that appear in that split's impressions -- so the full catalog
    is the union across splits. Articles appearing in both are deduplicated
    by news_id, keeping the first occurrence (an article's content doesn't
    change between splits).
    """
    combined = pd.concat(news_frames, ignore_index=True)
    combined = combined.drop_duplicates(subset="news_id", keep="first")

    articles = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "article_id": combined["news_id"],
            "category": combined["category"],
            "subcategory": combined["subcategory"],
            "title": combined["title"],
            # Missing abstracts (~5% of articles) become an empty string
            # rather than dropping the article: losing real catalog items
            # over one optional field would silently shrink recall for
            # every retrieval method built on top of this table.
            "abstract": combined["abstract"].fillna(""),
        }
    )
    # `text` is the single field BM25 and embeddings will actually index --
    # computed once here so every retrieval method sees an identical corpus.
    articles["text"] = (articles["title"] + " " + articles["abstract"]).str.strip()

    return articles[ARTICLES_COLUMNS].reset_index(drop=True)


def _parse_history(history: object) -> list:
    """Turn a raw space-separated history string (or NaN) into a list of IDs."""
    if pd.isna(history):
        return []
    return history.split()


def build_impressions_and_interactions(
    *behaviors_frames: pd.DataFrame,
) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Explode raw MIND behaviors frames into normalized impressions + interactions.

    `impressions` holds one row per impression (its user, time, and click
    history); `interactions` holds one row per (impression, candidate
    article, clicked) pair. Splitting these into two tables, rather than
    repeating `history` on every candidate row, avoids duplicating a
    dozens-of-items list across every candidate of the same impression.
    """
    behaviors = pd.concat(behaviors_frames, ignore_index=True)

    impressions = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "impression_id": behaviors["impression_id"],
            "user_id": behaviors["user_id"],
            "time": behaviors["time"],
            "history": behaviors["history"].apply(_parse_history),
        }
    )[IMPRESSIONS_COLUMNS].reset_index(drop=True)

    # Explode "N20678-0 N39317-0 ..." into one row per candidate. Vectorized
    # string ops here, rather than a Python loop, because this runs over
    # tens of thousands of impressions with dozens of candidates each.
    candidate_pairs = behaviors["impressions"].str.split()
    exploded = behaviors[["impression_id"]].join(candidate_pairs.rename("pair")).explode("pair")
    # rsplit from the right, once: article IDs never contain "-", but
    # splitting from the label side is the robust way to write this either way.
    split_pair = exploded["pair"].str.rsplit("-", n=1, expand=True)

    interactions = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "impression_id": exploded["impression_id"],
            "article_id": split_pair[0],
            "clicked": split_pair[1].astype("int8"),
        }
    )[INTERACTIONS_COLUMNS].reset_index(drop=True)

    return impressions, interactions

    # `text` is the single field BM25 and embeddings will actually index --
    # computed once here so every retrieval method sees an identical corpus.
    articles["text"] = (articles["title"] + " " + articles["abstract"]).str.strip()

    return articles[ARTICLES_COLUMNS].reset_index(drop=True)


def _parse_history(history: object) -> list:
    """Turn a raw space-separated history string (or NaN) into a list of IDs."""
    if pd.isna(history):
        return []
    return history.split()


def build_impressions_and_interactions(
    *behaviors_frames: pd.DataFrame,
) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Explode raw MIND behaviors frames into normalized impressions + interactions.

    `impressions` holds one row per impression (its user, time, and click
    history); `interactions` holds one row per (impression, candidate
    article, clicked) pair. Splitting these into two tables, rather than
    repeating `history` on every candidate row, avoids duplicating a
    dozens-of-items list across every candidate of the same impression.
    """
    behaviors = pd.concat(behaviors_frames, ignore_index=True)

    impressions = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "impression_id": behaviors["impression_id"],
            "user_id": behaviors["user_id"],
            "time": behaviors["time"],
            "history": behaviors["history"].apply(_parse_history),
        }
    )[IMPRESSIONS_COLUMNS].reset_index(drop=True)

    # Explode "N20678-0 N39317-0 ..." into one row per candidate. Vectorized
    # string ops here, rather than a Python loop, because this runs over
    # tens of thousands of impressions with dozens of candidates each.
    candidate_pairs = behaviors["impressions"].str.split()
    exploded = behaviors[["impression_id"]].join(candidate_pairs.rename("pair")).explode("pair")
    # rsplit from the right, once: article IDs never contain "-", but
    # splitting from the label side is the robust way to write this either way.
    split_pair = exploded["pair"].str.rsplit("-", n=1, expand=True)

    interactions = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "impression_id": exploded["impression_id"],
            "article_id": split_pair[0],
            "clicked": split_pair[1].astype("int8"),
        }
    )[INTERACTIONS_COLUMNS].reset_index(drop=True)

    return impressions, interactions

"""Clean raw MIND-small train/dev files into the project's common schema.

Reads data/raw/mind_small/{train,dev}/.../{news,behaviors}.tsv, unions and
normalizes them, and writes three parquet tables to data/interim/mind_small/:
articles.parquet, impressions.parquet, interactions.parquet.

Usage:
    python scripts/clean_mind.py --config configs/mind_small.yaml
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse

from news_reco.data.mind_adapter import build_articles_table, build_impressions_and_interactions
from news_reco.data.mind_loader import load_behaviors, load_news
from news_reco.utils.config import PipelineConfig, load_config


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--config", required=True, help="Path to a dataset YAML config.")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    config: PipelineConfig = load_config(args.config)

    train_dir = config.raw_dir / "train" / "MINDsmall_train"
    dev_dir = config.raw_dir / "dev" / "MINDsmall_dev"

    print("Loading raw files ...")
    train_news = load_news(train_dir / "news.tsv")
    dev_news = load_news(dev_dir / "news.tsv")
    train_behaviors = load_behaviors(train_dir / "behaviors.tsv")
    dev_behaviors = load_behaviors(dev_dir / "behaviors.tsv")

    print("Building common-schema tables ...")
    articles = build_articles_table(train_news, dev_news)
    impressions, interactions = build_impressions_and_interactions(train_behaviors, dev_behaviors)

    config.interim_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    articles.to_parquet(config.interim_dir / "articles.parquet", index=False)
    impressions.to_parquet(config.interim_dir / "impressions.parquet", index=False)
    interactions.to_parquet(config.interim_dir / "interactions.parquet", index=False)

    dedup_count = (len(train_news) + len(dev_news)) - len(articles)
    print(f"\narticles:     {len(articles):,} rows ({dedup_count:,} duplicates removed across train/dev)")
    print(f"impressions:  {len(impressions):,} rows")
    print(f"interactions: {len(interactions):,} rows")
    print(f"click rate:   {interactions['clicked'].mean():.4f}")
    print(f"empty text (title+abstract both blank): {(articles['text'] == '').sum():,}")
    print(f"\nWrote parquet files to {config.interim_dir}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

**Next**
- Milestone 2: cleaning & normalization into the common schema (articles

---

## Milestone 2 — Cleaning & normalization into the common schema (2026-08-02)

**What was built**
- `src/news_reco/data/schema.py`: column definitions for three
  dataset-agnostic tables — `articles`, `impressions`, `interactions`. Every
  future dataset adapter (MIND now, EB-NeRD later) must produce exactly
  these columns, so everything downstream (splitting, features, retrieval,
  evaluation) is written once, not once per dataset.
- `src/news_reco/data/mind_adapter.py`: `build_articles_table()` (union +
  dedupe train/dev news.tsv by `news_id`, missing abstract → `""`, derives a
  `text` field = title+abstract) and `build_impressions_and_interactions()`
  (explodes each impression's candidate string into normalized
  `impressions` + `interactions` tables, avoiding repeating `history` on
  every candidate row).
- `tests/test_mind_adapter.py`: unit tests against small hand-crafted
  DataFrames with known-correct expected outputs (dedup, missing-abstract
  fallback, explode correctness) — independent of whether the real dataset
  is downloaded.
- `scripts/clean_mind.py`: runs the adapter against the real downloaded
  data and writes `data/interim/mind_small/{articles,impressions,interactions}.parquet`.

**Design decisions**
- **Freshness/"first seen" gating deferred to Milestone 6**, not built now.
  MIND's `news.tsv` has no publish-date column at all (only EB-NeRD ships
  real timestamps), so any freshness signal for MIND would have to be a
  proxy (e.g. earliest time an article appears in any impression) — that's
  a genuine judgment call tied to *how candidates get gated during
  retrieval*, not to *what "clean" data looks like*, so it belongs with
  candidate-generation logic (M6), not cleaning (M2). Flagging this now so
  it isn't forgotten, and because it directly touches the assignment's
  anti-gaming "no future-click leakage" requirement.
- **Missing abstract → empty string, article kept** (not dropped). ~5% of
  articles have no abstract; dropping them would shrink the retrievable
  catalog and silently hurt every method's recall ceiling over a data
  formatting quirk, not a real data quality problem.
- **`impressions` and `interactions` kept as two normalized tables**
  (joined by `impression_id`) instead of one denormalized table repeating
  `history` per candidate row — standard normalization, avoids repeating a
  dozens-of-items list across every candidate of the same impression.

**Observations**
- 65,238 unique articles after deduplication (28,460 duplicate rows removed
  across train ∪ dev — confirms the two splits' catalogs overlap heavily,
  as expected for a 6-day window).
- 230,117 impressions total (156,965 + 73,152, matches Milestone 1 exactly).
- 8,584,442 candidate rows in `interactions` (~37 candidates/impression on
  average).
- **Click rate: 4.05%** — matches published MIND baseline statistics from
  the literature, a useful external sanity check that nothing is
  systematically miscounted.
- Zero articles ended up with fully empty `text` (title alone always
  covers what abstract-fallback leaves).
- Referential integrity verified: every `interactions.article_id` exists in
  `articles.article_id` (no orphaned candidate references).

**Limitations**
- Parquet round-trips the `history` list column as a `numpy.ndarray`, not a
  Python `list`, once read back — functionally equivalent (`len()`,
  indexing, iteration all work) but anything doing an `== [...]` equality
  check against a re-loaded `history` value needs `.tolist()` first. Noted
  here so it doesn't cause a confusing test failure later.
